text: Design encode, to turn a list of strings into one string, and decode, to recover the exact list. No built-in serialization. Strings may contain any of the two hundred fifty-six ASCII characters.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Since a string can contain literally any character — including whatever I'd want as a separator — I can't just join with a delimiter. Empty strings are allowed too? And the follow-up asks it to work for any character set?
Right on all counts — empties allowed, and yes, make it general.

Then a plain delimiter is out: a single string, a comma b, would be split into two. The robust approach is length-prefixed framing — write each string's length before it, and decode by reading exactly that many characters.

Let me reason about why this is safe. This problem reminds me of the length-prefix, or type-length-value, framing used in network protocols, and it fits for the same reason. Each chunk is a length, an at sign, then the payload. On decode, the pointer always sits at a length, which is pure digits, so the first at sign is guaranteed to be the framing marker — never a payload character. I then read the payload by count, so it never gets scanned. That works for any character set.

Here's the plan. One: encode each string as its length, an at sign, and the string. Two: to decode, find the next at sign from i and parse the digits before it as the length. Three: take exactly that many characters after it, then jump i past the whole chunk. Two things worth flagging. First, the delimiter must be a non-digit, like the at sign, so it can't blend into the length. Second, the loop invariant: i always lands on the next length, because I jump the whole payload. Empty strings fall out for free — a length of zero reads zero characters. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. Encode loops over the strings and appends the length, an at sign, and the payload. Decode keeps a pointer i: find the at sign, turn the digits between i and j into len, cut len characters after the at sign, and move on. That matches the plan. One detail worth flagging — i equals j plus one plus len skips over the entire payload, so any at sign inside it is never even looked at by find. Forget the plus one, or the len, and the pointer lands mid-chunk.

Let's dry-run a payload that contains the delimiter: cat, n-at-p, hi, which encodes to three-at-cat, three-at-n-at-p, two-at-hi. The highlighted row is the point: find from index five returns six, not the at sign at index eight inside n-at-p — because index five starts a length. We read three characters and jump to ten, so the inner at sign is pure data. Corner cases: a list with one empty string encodes to zero-at and comes back, since length zero reads nothing. A string of all at signs round-trips. NUL bytes round-trip. All check out.

Decode is linear in L, the total number of characters — each character is read a constant number of times. Space is order L for the output, and the length prefix adds only a few bytes per string. One thing worth flagging on encode: enc equals enc plus the chunk copies the whole string built so far, every time; plus-equals appends in place and keeps encode linear too. One more thing — for a binary protocol I'd use a fixed-width length, say four bytes, instead of digits plus delimiter — no non-digit assumption, faster to parse. And this framing composes: nesting lists just wraps another length prefix around each encoded sublist.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: seeing that a delimiter fails on adversarial payloads, the length-prefix invariant that keeps the pointer on a length, and reading the payload by count so any character is safe — plus the fixed-width and nesting extensions. Good work.
